title: Can you have two `main()` methods in a Spring/Java application (one per class, multiple classes allowed)?
shortTitle: Can you have two main methods in a Java application?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes, a Java or Spring application can contain many classes, and each class may declare its own public static void main of a String array, so an application can have dozens of valid entry points. This is entirely normal because the entry point is resolved per class: the JVM starts whichever class you name on the command line and invokes that class's main. What a single class cannot have is two identical main signatures, since that would be a duplicate method and fail to compile. In a Spring application you typically have one primary main annotated class that boots the context, but additional classes with their own main are allowed and common for batch jobs, utilities, and command-line tools, and the build tool simply needs to know which one is the default main class to launch.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the whole bank is one application, but it has many branches, and each branch can have its own official opening-time front door, meaning its own main. Head office, meaning the JVM, opens exactly one branch at a time by naming it, and that branch's door is used. So the bank can have a main door for the core online banking branch, another for the nightly settlement branch, and another for a reporting utility branch, all in the same bank. What a single branch cannot have is two identical front doors of the same shape, because then the builder, meaning the compiler, would not know which to install. The build tool is like the directory that records which branch is the default one to open when someone just says open the bank.
s1_definition.oneliner: Yes, you can have many main methods, one per class, because entry points are resolved per class; a single class just cannot declare two identical main signatures, and the build tool records which class is the default to launch.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes, a Java or Spring application can contain many classes, and each class may declare its own public static void main of a String array, so an application can have dozens of valid entry points. This is entirely normal because the entry point is resolved per class: the JVM starts whichever class you name on the command line and invokes that class's main. What a single class cannot have is two identical main signatures, since that would be a duplicate method and fail to compile. In a Spring application you typically have one primary main annotated class that boots the context, but additional classes with their own main are allowed and common for batch jobs, utilities, and command-line tools, and the build tool simply needs to know which one is the default main class to launch.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the whole bank is one application, but it has many branches, and each branch can have its own official opening-time front door, meaning its own main. Head office, meaning the JVM, opens exactly one branch at a time by naming it, and that branch's door is used. So the bank can have a main door for the core online banking branch, another for the nightly settlement branch, and another for a reporting utility branch, all in the same bank. What a single branch cannot have is two identical front doors of the same shape, because then the builder, meaning the compiler, would not know which to install. The build tool is like the directory that records which branch is the default one to open when someone just says open the bank.

**One line to remember:** Yes, you can have many main methods, one per class, because entry points are resolved per class; a single class just cannot declare two identical main signatures, and the build tool records which class is the default to launch.

sections.s2_technical:
The JVM entry-point rule is per class. When you run a program you name a specific class, and the launcher invokes that class's public static void main of a String array. There is nothing preventing many different classes in the same project from each declaring that signature, so an application can legitimately have many entry points. This is not overloading and not overriding; they are simply independent classes each with their own main.

A single class, however, cannot contain two methods with the identical signature public static void main of a String array, because Java does not allow two methods with the same name and parameter list in one class; that is a duplicate method compile error. A class can contain overloaded mains with different parameters, as discussed separately, but only one of them is the actual String array entry point.

In plain Java this flexibility is used constantly. A project might have a MainApp class for the primary application, a BatchSettlement class with its own main for the nightly job, and a ReportTool class with its own main for ad hoc reports. You choose which to run by naming the class, for example java with the fully qualified class name, and the chosen class's main executes. When packaging a runnable jar, the manifest's Main-Class attribute records the single default entry point used when you run the jar without naming a class, but you can still run any other main by naming its class on the classpath.

In a Spring Boot application the pattern is the same with a conventional default. The primary entry point is a class annotated with at-SpringBootApplication whose main calls SpringApplication.run, which bootstraps the entire application context, auto-configuration, and embedded server. That is normally the one default main. But it is perfectly legal and common to have additional classes with their own main for standalone batch jobs or tools that may or may not start a Spring context. The Spring Boot build plugin asks you to designate the main class when there is more than one, via the start-class property in Maven or the mainClass in the Gradle configuration, so the packaged jar knows which main to launch by default.

Several senior points matter. First, having multiple mains is a clean way to ship several runnable tools from one codebase while sharing domain code, which is exactly how banks package a core service plus several operational utilities. Second, the build must disambiguate the default main, and forgetting to do so produces a build error that multiple main classes were found, which is a routine and easily fixed configuration issue. Third, in a Spring Boot context you should generally have exactly one class that calls SpringApplication.run for the running service, because booting two contexts in one process is unusual, while secondary mains for standalone tools typically do not start the web context. Fourth, modular build setups often split each runnable into its own module to keep the entry points and their dependencies clean. The practical upshot is that multiple mains are allowed and useful; the discipline is to configure the default entry point explicitly and to keep the Spring boot main distinct from utility mains.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank ships one codebase that must run both as the main online service and as a separate nightly settlement job, each started independently. This is exactly why multiple classes each with their own main are allowed.

Problem 2 — The operations team runs the settlement job directly by naming its class, without starting the whole online service. This is exactly per-class entry-point resolution.

Problem 3 — When the project is packaged into a runnable jar, the build must know which main is the default, or it reports multiple main classes found. This is exactly the need to designate the default entry point.

The code provides two independent classes, an `OnlineBankingApp` main simulating the primary service entry point and a `SettlementJob` main simulating the standalone batch entry point, both in the same application, plus the build configuration note designating the default.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
multi-main-demo/
├── pom.xml                         (designates the default main class)
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/app/
│       ├── OnlineBankingApp.java   (primary entry point — would call SpringApplication.run)
│       └── SettlementJob.java      (standalone batch entry point — its own main)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile both entry-point classes
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/app/OnlineBankingApp.java \
             src/main/java/com/bank/app/SettlementJob.java

# Run the PRIMARY service by naming its class
java -cp out com.bank.app.OnlineBankingApp

# Run the STANDALONE batch by naming its class (same codebase)
java -cp out com.bank.app.SettlementJob 2026-10-30

# Packaged jar uses the designated default main (OnlineBankingApp):
java -jar target/multi-main-demo-1.0.0.jar
# ...but you can still launch the batch by naming its class on the classpath:
java -cp target/multi-main-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.app.SettlementJob 2026-10-30
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the choice of which class to run, and for the batch a settlement date argument.

Step 1 — The project contains two classes, each with its own valid public static void main of a String array. Both are legitimate entry points because the entry point is resolved per class, not per application.

Step 2 — When the operations team runs the primary service, they name OnlineBankingApp on the command line. The JVM loads that class and invokes its main, which in a real Spring Boot application would call the run method to boot the context and start the embedded server serving the REST APIs.

Step 3 — When the team instead runs the nightly batch, they name SettlementJob. The JVM loads that class and invokes its main, which reads the date argument and performs the settlement, typically without starting the web context. The online service and the batch never collide because only the named class's main runs.

Step 4 — When the project is packaged into a runnable jar, the build plugin writes the designated default main class, OnlineBankingApp, into the jar manifest. Running the jar without naming a class therefore starts the primary service.

Step 5 — Even with the default set, the team can still run the batch from the same jar by naming SettlementJob on the classpath, demonstrating that all mains remain reachable while one is the default.

Step 6 — The output differs by which class was named: naming the service prints the service startup messages, and naming the batch prints the settlement messages for the given date, proving multiple mains coexist peacefully.

```
# java com.bank.app.OnlineBankingApp
Oct 30, 2026 5:18:03 PM com.bank.app.OnlineBankingApp main
INFO: OnlineBankingApp.main() — DEFAULT entry point.
INFO: Would call SpringApplication.run(...) to boot context + embedded server.
INFO: Serves REST APIs for transfers, balances, statements.

# java com.bank.app.SettlementJob 2026-10-30
Oct 30, 2026 5:18:09 PM com.bank.app.SettlementJob main
INFO: SettlementJob.main() — standalone batch entry point for 2026-10-30
INFO: Settling Rs.50000.00 transfers from SAV2001 to CUR3001
INFO: Settlement batch complete.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  One codebase, many entry points (one main per class)
    │
    ├─ java com.bank.app.OnlineBankingApp
    │     │ JVM loads OnlineBankingApp → its static main
    │     ▼
    │   boot Spring context + REST server (DEFAULT)
    │
    └─ java com.bank.app.SettlementJob 2026-10-30
          │ JVM loads SettlementJob → its static main
          ▼
        run nightly settlement batch (no web context)

  Packaged jar:
    manifest Main-Class = com.bank.app.OnlineBankingApp  ← default
    java -jar app.jar                 → OnlineBankingApp
    java -cp app.jar ...SettlementJob → SettlementJob (still reachable)

  A SINGLE class with TWO identical main(String[]) → COMPILE ERROR (duplicate method)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, a Java or Spring application can absolutely have multiple main methods, as long as they live in different classes, because the entry point is resolved per class. When you launch, you name a specific class and the JVM invokes that class's public static void main of a String array. So nothing prevents many classes in one project from each declaring that signature, and an application can legitimately have several entry points. The one thing a single class cannot do is declare two identical main signatures, because Java forbids two methods with the same name and parameter list in one class, which is just a duplicate method compile error.

In plain Java I use this all the time to ship several runnable tools from one codebase. A project might have a primary application class, a batch settlement class with its own main for the nightly job, and a reporting tool class with its own main, all sharing the same domain code. I choose which to run simply by naming the class on the command line, and the named class's main executes. When I package a runnable jar, the manifest's Main-Class attribute records the single default entry point used when the jar is run without naming a class, but I can still launch any other main by naming its class on the classpath.

In Spring Boot it is the same idea with a conventional default. The primary entry point is the class annotated with at-SpringBootApplication whose main calls SpringApplication.run, which boots the whole context, auto-configuration, and embedded server, and that is normally the one running service. It is perfectly legal and common to have additional classes with their own main for standalone batch jobs or utilities, and those typically do not start the web context. The Spring Boot build plugin just needs me to designate the default main class when there is more than one, through the main class setting in Maven or Gradle, so the packaged jar knows which to launch by default.

In our banking system this is exactly how we ship one codebase that runs both as the online service and as a separate nightly settlement job. The senior points I add are that multiple mains are a clean way to share domain code across several runnable tools, that the build must explicitly disambiguate the default or it reports multiple main classes found, which is a routine configuration fix, and that I keep exactly one class calling the Spring run method for the running service while the secondary mains for tools stay standalone. So the answer is a confident yes with one caveat: many mains across classes are allowed and useful, but a single class has exactly one String array entry point, and the build should name the default explicitly.

---

keyPoints: Yes — each class can have its own main(String[] args)
JVM runs the one you specify: java com.bank.MyClass
In Spring Boot, @SpringBootApplication designates the entry class
Multiple mains useful for module-level testing or demos
